The same applies to your career: professionals who play the long game — investing in skills, relationships, and reputation even when there's no immediate payoff — eventually operate on a completely different plane to those who optimise quarter-by-quarter.

cards.headline: Short Game vs Long Game
cards.body: 80,000 Hours' research reveals that career satisfaction and compensation diverge sharply after 10+ years based on early strategic choices:
bullets: Short game: Chase the highest immediate salary → gets stuck at mid-level ceiling, limited by narrow skill set
Long game: Accept slightly lower early pay for learning, range, and positioning → breaks through to senior/executive level
Short game: Avoid risk → never builds the signal that distinguishes leaders
Long game: Take calculated risks early (when the cost of failure is low) → builds reputation and confidence

cards.headline: The Regret Minimisation Framework
cards.body: Bezos decided to leave a cushy Wall Street job for Amazon using his "regret minimisation framework": he imagined himself at 80 and asked "Will I regret NOT trying this?" Apply this to career decisions: when choosing between the safe-but-stagnant path and the risky-but-growth path, the 80-year-old version of you will almost always regret playing it safe. Time is your greatest asset — don't waste it on comfort.

cards.headline: Building a Career Moat
cards.body: A career moat is what makes you irreplaceable. It's built from: 1) A unique skill combination nobody else has (your skill stack). 2) A reputation that precedes you (the flywheel from Lesson 18). 3) A network that opens doors others can't access. 4) Institutional knowledge or relationships that took years to build. The deeper your moat, the more leverage you have — and the less negotiation you ever need to do.

cards.headline: Write Your 10-Year Letter
cards.body: Write a letter from your future self, 10 years from now, to present-day you. Describe: What role do you have? What do you earn? What did it take to get there? What risks were worth taking? What would you tell yourself to start doing NOW? Be specific and ambitious. Then reverse-engineer: what needs to happen in years 1-3 to make the year-10 vision possible? That's your long game strategy.

quiz.question: What does "playing the long game" mean for career strategy?
options: Investing in skills, relationships, and positioning even without immediate payoff
Staying at the same company forever to build tenure
Always accepting the highest-paying job offer available
Waiting patiently for promotion without taking any action
quiz.explanation: The long game means making decisions that compound over time — learning new skills, building relationships, taking calculated risks, developing a reputation — even when there's no immediate salary bump. After 10+ years, long-game players operate on an entirely different earning curve.

quiz.question: Always choosing the highest-paying option is the best long-term career strategy.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Research shows that always chasing the highest immediate salary often leads to mid-level ceiling stagnation. Accepting slightly lower early pay for better learning, broader skills, and stronger positioning frequently leads to much higher long-term compensation by enabling breakthrough to senior/executive levels.

quiz.question: What is a "career moat"?
options: A unique combination of skills, reputation, network, and knowledge that makes you irreplaceable
A large gap between your salary and your colleagues' salaries
Having so much savings that you never need to work again
Being the longest-tenured person in your department
quiz.explanation: A career moat — like a business moat — is what makes you defensible and irreplaceable. It's built from unique skill combinations, a strong reputation, an expansive network, and deep knowledge that took years to accumulate. The deeper the moat, the more natural leverage you command.

lessons.title: Course Finale
lessons.subtitle: You now have a complete system for earning what you're worth — for the rest of your career.

cards.headline: You've Built a Career Operating System
cards.body: Twenty-one days ago, most professionals were winging their careers — hoping great work would be noticed, accepting whatever was offered, and wondering why others got promoted faster. You now have what they don't: a complete system for knowing your worth, asking for it effectively, and compounding your career capital over decades. This isn't a one-time fix — it's a permanent upgrade to how you operate.

cards.headline: Your Complete System (Summary)
cards.body: Your Salary & Promotion Playbook system has three layers that work together:
bullets: Module 1 (Foundation): Market research, decision map, evidence portfolio, timing, visibility — you never walk into a conversation unprepared again
Module 2 (Negotiation): Tactical empathy, mirroring, calibrated questions, anchoring, ACRE framework, handling "no" — you have FBI-level negotiation skills
Module 3 (Compounding): First 90 days, sponsors, executive presence, skill stacking, career moat — your earning power compounds exponentially over time

cards.headline: The Numbers That Changed
cards.body: If you apply this system once — just one successful negotiation — the typical outcome is a 10-20% compensation increase. Over a 30-year career, a single 15% bump in year one (invested at 7% return) is worth over £1M in lifetime earnings and retirement savings. But you won't use this just once. You'll use it at every job change, every review, every promotion. The compound effect is staggering.
cards.statLabel: lifetime value of a single successful salary negotiation early in your career

cards.headline: Your Ongoing Cadence
cards.body: Keep this system alive with a simple ongoing cadence: Weekly — update your brag document (5 min). Monthly — have a visibility touchpoint with one decision-maker. Quarterly — review your market value and sponsor relationships. Annually — have the conversation (or negotiate a move). The system only fails if you stop maintaining it. The investment is tiny — the returns are life-changing.

cards.headline: Your First Negotiation Commitment
cards.body: Make a specific commitment: "Within the next [30/60/90] days, I will have a compensation or promotion conversation using the ACRE framework." Write the date. Tell someone (accountability partner, friend, or even just write it in your calendar as a recurring reminder). Then: begin your preparation immediately — update your brag document, refresh your market data, and identify your first conversation partner. You have everything you need. Now act.

quiz.question: What is the estimated lifetime value of a single successful salary negotiation early in your career?
options: Over £1M in earnings and retirement savings when compounded over 30 years
About £5,000-£10,000 in the first year
Negligible — salary increases only matter at senior levels
Impossible to estimate without knowing your exact role
quiz.explanation: A 15% salary increase early in your career, compounded over 30 years (through subsequent raises on a higher base plus investment returns), typically exceeds £1M in lifetime value. This is why negotiation skills are arguably the highest-ROI investment a professional can make.

quiz.question: Once you've completed this course, the system works automatically without maintenance.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The system requires a simple ongoing cadence: weekly brag document updates (5 min), monthly visibility touchpoints, quarterly market/sponsor reviews, and annual compensation conversations. The investment is minimal but essential — an unmaintained system atrophies.

quiz.question: What ongoing cadence keeps the Salary & Promotion system active?
options: Weekly brag doc, monthly visibility, quarterly market review, annual conversation
Daily negotiations with your manager
Yearly performance review preparation only
Monthly job applications to maintain leverage
quiz.explanation: The ongoing cadence is lightweight but consistent: weekly evidence capture (5 min), monthly stakeholder touchpoints, quarterly market and sponsor relationship reviews, and an annual compensation conversation. This keeps all three system layers — preparation, negotiation, compounding — active and effective.
